Live

Rome, late November. A national TV channel holds a debate about the T under Caravaggio's signature. In the studio: Giulia and Professor Ruggeri, a sceptical art historian. The presenter is Elena Marchi.
Professor Ruggeri, you wrote that the story of the T is "a fairy tale for tourists". Why?
Because, in my view, a drop of paint is not a letter. I have the impression that someone wanted to see what they wished to see.
Not that I want to contradict you, professor, but we never said it was proof. We said it was a clue.
A clue found by a twelve-year-old on a scaffold. Doesn't that seem a bit like a novel to you?
I don't deny it's a story like a novel. But the fact remains that Agata and Salvatore were in Malta in September 1608. There's a document.
As far as I know, in Malta in 1608 there were hundreds of Sicilian washerwomen. It's not certain it was the same Agata.
Of course. But with a seven-year-old son called Salvatore, in the same month, in the same city as the painter? I'm convinced it's at least worth studying.
Professor, it's undeniable that there are a lot of coincidences.
Coincidences don't make art history. The point is that without a chemical analysis, we know nothing.
On that we agree completely. And that's exactly what we're proposing.
Ah. Then, as far as I'm concerned, the discussion becomes interesting.

La T in televisione

The news of the T reached the Italian papers in mid-November, after Rosalia Lo Bianco had published a short article in an academic journal. At first it seemed a curiosity for specialists. Then a Milan weekly put an enlarged photo of Caravaggio's signature on its cover, with the little T circled in red and a huge headline: "Did Caravaggio's secret child sign with him?". In three days the story was on every website. In five, it was on the TV news. And on the sixth day a phone call came to the workshop in Via Maggio from Rome.

It was the production team of a national TV talk show, "Ne parliamo stasera", which every Thursday set two guests against each other on a topical subject. They wanted Giulia, live, the following week. Against her, they said, would be Professor Ruggeri, an art historian at the University of Rome, who in the press had called the story of the T "a fairy tale for tourists, good for selling postcards". Giulia was silent on the phone for a few seconds. Then she said she would think about it. She hung up and looked at Matei. "On television," she said. "Against a professor. Me, who used to tremble when I was tested at school."

The family council met that very evening, at the trattoria. Opinions were divided. Graziella was against it: for her, television was "a place where people shout and nobody listens", and she didn't see why Giulia should go and be shouted at by a professor from Rome. Marco was in favour: in his view, if Giulia didn't go, Ruggeri would talk alone and the story would become his. Bellini, from his table, listened without saying anything. Pietro, who felt partly responsible because he was the one who had seen the T, was the most agitated of all.

Later, when the others had gone, Pietro stayed in the kitchen with his grandmother. "It's my fault," he said. "If I hadn't seen that T, nobody would be talking about fairy tales for tourists." Graziella put down her ladle. "It's not that it's your fault," she replied. "It's to your credit. Which is different." Pietro didn't seem convinced. So Graziella told him that when her father opened the trattoria in 1952, half the neighbourhood said it would go bust within a year, because ribollita was "poor people's food". "My dad didn't argue with anyone," she said. "He cooked. And after a year the people who said it was poor people's food came to eat it every day. Gossip passes, Pietro. Things done well remain."

In the end it was Bellini who spoke. "I know Ruggeri," he said. "We studied together, forty years ago. He's not a bad man. He's a sceptic, which is something else. Sceptics are useful: they force you to prove what you say." He paused. "The problem isn't Ruggeri. The problem is that you, Giulia, must go there knowing exactly what you want to argue. Not that the T is proof. It isn't. But that it's a clue that deserves to be studied. If you say that, and only that, nobody will be able to take you apart."

For a week the trattoria became a debating gym. Every evening after dinner Pietro played Ruggeri, with a pair of fake glasses and a deep voice, and Giulia had to answer him. Valeria Conti, who knew a thing or two about difficult meetings, taught Giulia the rules: don't interrupt, don't raise your voice, always concede something before contradicting. "Never say 'you're wrong'," she explained. "Say 'I don't deny you're right on this point, but…'. Your opponent lowers his guard, and you can strike." Graziella, from the kitchen, remarked that it sounded like a boxing lesson.

On the evening of the broadcast, all of Via Maggio was in front of the television. In the trattoria Marco had moved the tables and switched on the old television above the counter, the one used for Fiorentina matches. There were Graziella, Bellini, Chiara, Davide with his parents, Signor Franco, Lorenzo, Rita, Valeria. Even Lupino seemed to understand that something important was happening, and lay motionless under the table with his ears pricked. Pietro, on the other hand, was in Rome: Giulia had taken him with her, "because you saw the T, and you must see what becomes of it".

The studio was smaller than Pietro had imagined, and terribly hot because of the lights. He sat in the front row of the audience, between a lady in a fur coat and a student with a notebook. The presenter, Elena Marchi, an elegant woman with a soft voice and sharp questions, introduced the guests. Professor Ruggeri was a tall man with a well-groomed white beard and a polite smile that didn't reach his eyes. Giulia, next to him, looked small, but Pietro noticed she kept her hands still on her knees. It was the sign, Valeria had taught her, that she wouldn't tremble.

Half an hour before going on air, in the make-up room, Giulia had confessed to Pietro that she was scared. A make-up artist was powdering her nose, and she was looking at her reflection in the mirror the way you look at a stranger. "What if I freeze?" she said. "What if he asks me something and I don't know the answer?" Pietro thought for a moment. Then he took from his pocket Ernesto's small brush, which Bellini had lent him specially for that evening, wrapped in the usual handkerchief. "The professor said to give it to you," he explained. "He said if you freeze, you must think of it like restoring: one millimetre at a time. One sentence at a time." Giulia laughed, for the first time in days, and the make-up artist had to redo her lipstick.

Ruggeri attacked straight away, elegantly. "In my view," he said, "we're looking at a classic case. A drop of paint, a moving story, a young boy, a grandmother, a ribollita. All very nice. But art history isn't made with emotions. I have the impression that someone, in good faith, saw what they wanted to see." The audience murmured. In the trattoria in Florence, Graziella said loudly that the ribollita had nothing to do with it, and Bellini asked her to be quiet. Pietro, in the studio, clenched his fists.

Just at that moment the presenter announced the commercial break. The lights dimmed, the technicians started running around with cables, and Giulia sat still with her eyes closed. Pietro saw her take something from her jacket pocket: the handkerchief with Ernesto's brush. She held it for a few seconds without opening it, then put it back. Ruggeri, beside her, was drinking a glass of water and checking his notes. For a moment their eyes met. Ruggeri gave a small nod, almost a greeting between colleagues. Giulia returned it. Pietro, in the front row, had the strange feeling that the real debate was only now about to begin.

Giulia waited until the professor had finished. Then she smiled. "Not that I want to contradict you, professor," she said calmly. "On the contrary, you're right about many things. I don't deny the story is moving, and I don't deny emotions can deceive. But we never said the T was proof. We said, and I repeat it here, that it's a clue. A clue which, on its own, is worth nothing. But the fact remains that in the register of the knights' hospital, in September 1608, there's a Sicilian washerwoman called Agata, with a seven-year-old son called Salvatore."

Ruggeri was not thrown. "As far as I know," he replied, "in Malta in 1608 there were hundreds of Sicilian washerwomen. And Salvatore was one of the commonest names on the island. It's not certain it was the same Agata as in Syracuse." "Of course," said Giulia. "I grant you that, taken one by one, none of these things proves anything. But taken together? A washerwoman called Agata, with a son called Salvatore, aged seven, in the same city and the same month as Caravaggio, who two months later paints in Syracuse a child the documents call Salvatore, son of Agata. I'm convinced it's at least worth studying."

There was a silence. The presenter turned to the professor. "Professor, it's undeniable that there are many coincidences," she said. Ruggeri stroked his beard. "Coincidences don't make art history," he replied. "The point is that, without a chemical analysis of the pigment, we know nothing. It could be a letter, a drop that fell by chance, an eighteenth-century retouch. Without analysis, it's all fantasy." Giulia nodded slowly. "On that," she said, "we agree completely. And that's exactly what we're proposing: a non-invasive analysis of the T, with the same technique used for the signature."

Ruggeri looked at her in surprise. He had expected, perhaps, a restorer defending a fairy tale. Instead he found himself facing a colleague asking for the same thing he was. "Ah," he said after a moment. And for the first time in the whole programme his smile reached his eyes. "Then, as far as I'm concerned, the discussion becomes interesting. If the analysis is done properly, I'm ready to change my mind. And if the T really turned out to be a letter in the same pigment as the signature…" He paused. "…I'd be the first to write it."

In the trattoria in Florence, applause broke out that made Lupino bark. Bellini took off his glasses and said only: "Well done. She did exactly what she had to do. She didn't win. She turned her opponent into an ally." Graziella, who until then had kept her hands clasped as if in church, unclasped them and said that anyway that professor's beard was too well groomed for him to be a serious person. Valeria Conti laughed. "Signora," she said, "it's the best debate I've ever seen on television. And nobody raised their voice."

After the programme, in the studio corridors, Ruggeri went up to Giulia and Pietro. He held out his hand to Giulia. "Forgive me for the 'fairy tale for tourists'," he said. "It was a provocation. I wanted to see if you had arguments or just emotions." Then he looked at Pietro. "And you're the boy from the scaffolding." Pietro nodded, red to the ears. Ruggeri studied him for a moment. "Do you know the most important quality for an art historian?" he asked. Pietro shook his head. "Not to believe anything until you've seen it twice," said Ruggeri. "Have you seen the T twice?"

"Three times," replied Pietro. "And I drew it. I've got it here." He took the notebook from his pocket and opened it at the page with the T, with the little curve, the line and the dot. Ruggeri looked at the drawing for a long time, with the same attention he would have given a painting. Then he asked permission to photograph it. "It's not proof," he said, handing back the notebook. "But it's an excellent drawing. Precise. Without fantasy. As far as I know, it's the most serious thing produced so far in this whole story." Pietro couldn't answer. Giulia squeezed his shoulder.

The next day the newspaper headlines were different from the previous week's. "Caravaggio: the T will be analysed," wrote a Rome daily. "The sceptic and the restorer make peace live on air," ran the headline in the Gazzetta dell'Oltrarno, with an article by Mancini quoting the final exchange word for word. And a week later came the news everyone had been waiting for: the Co-Cathedral in Valletta had authorised a non-invasive analysis of the T, in the spring, under the joint supervision of Dr Esposito and Professor Ruggeri.

In Syracuse, meanwhile, Turi had watched the programme in the sacristy, on an old television brought over specially from the presbytery. The next day he phoned Rosalia Lo Bianco, for the first time in his life on his own initiative. "Professor," he said, "that professor with the beard said that without analysis it's all fantasy. He's right. But I'm old, and I don't understand analyses. Just tell me one thing: do you believe it?" Rosalia hesitated. Then she answered as Giulia would have: "Not that I'm sure, Turi. But I have the impression that yes, I believe it." Turi was silent for a moment. "That's enough for me," he said. "At eighty, an impression is worth as much as proof." And that evening he lit another candle in front of the painting.

Camilleri phoned Giulia that very evening. "I saw the programme," he said, laughing. "Marija shouted the whole time. Lina recorded it all and showed it to half the university. And Karl, the apprentice, has said he wants to study art history in Rome, with Ruggeri." He paused. "But do you know the best thing? Ruggeri called me this morning. He asked if there's room for him too in the apartment with the green gallarija, in the spring. I said yes. But that Signora Graziella has to bring the ribollita."

When Giulia and Pietro got back to Florence, Graziella was waiting for them at the trattoria door with her arms folded. She hugged Giulia, then Pietro, then said without preamble: "So. This professor with the beard. Is he going to Malta with you?" Giulia nodded. Graziella sighed. "Not that I've got anything against him," she said. "But the fact remains that he called my ribollita 'a fairy tale for tourists'." "Grandma," protested Pietro, "he didn't say that! He said the story of the T was…" Graziella raised a hand. "I understood perfectly well what he said," she replied. "When he tastes it, the ribollita, we'll see if it's a fairy tale."

That evening Pietro opened Bellini's black notebook, which was now his diary, and wrote the date. Then he sat for a long time with the pen in his hand, thinking about what to write. In the end he wrote a single sentence that summed up everything he had learned that week: "I saw a real debate. Nobody won, and both were right. In my view, it's the best way to end a discussion." Then he added underneath, in small letters: "Ruggeri says you mustn't believe anything until you've seen it twice. I've seen the T three times. So I believe it a little more."
